patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, memory problems, and behavioral change; partner concerned about possible 'Hashimoto's flare'
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old right-handed woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis (currently euthyroid on levothyroxine) and remote depression was brought to the emergency department by her partner after 12 days of progressive cognitive and behavioral changes. The patient, who is herself a nurse practitioner, had noticed about two weeks ago that she was having unusual difficulty remembering her patients' information at work, which she attributed to stress. Over the following several days her partner noticed she was becoming increasingly forgetful and confused, frequently asking repetitive questions. She then developed insomnia — lying awake all night despite exhaustion — followed by episodes of agitation and what her partner describes as 'talking nonsense.' In the 5 days prior to presentation she developed peculiar repetitive behaviors: repeatedly checking the front door lock, making the same gestures with her hands, and at times appearing to chew or swallow without food present. She had one brief episode (lasting approximately 40 seconds) where she was staring, unresponsive, and her right arm was rhythmically moving, after which she was confused and did not recall the episode. Her partner initially thought this might be a 'Hashimoto's encephalopathy' given her known thyroid autoimmunity, but her levothyroxine dose has not changed and her TSH was checked 6 weeks ago and was normal. She had a significant febrile illness with sore throat and myalgias about 6 weeks ago, which was diagnosed as a viral syndrome at an urgent care clinic. On arrival, the patient appears disheveled and is not at her usual functional level.

results.title: Hashimoto encephalopathy: a rare condition requiring CSF and antibody workup

results.key_finding: Elevated anti-TPO antibodies are present in a broad range of autoimmune conditions; the diagnosis of Hashimoto encephalopathy requires both elevated anti-thyroid antibodies and exclusion of other causes including antibody-mediated encephalitis

differential.key_features: Acute febrile encephalopathy with temporal-lobe focus; mandatory empiric acyclovir until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative.

differential.diagnosis: Other autoimmune (paraneoplastic) encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, or AMPAR)
differential.key_features: Limbic encephalitis phenotype with similar imaging; distinguished by surface-antigen antibody panel and demographic skew (LGI1/CASPR2 older men, GABA-B with SCLC, AMPAR with thymoma).
Subacute course, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis argue strongly against a primary psychiatric etiology.
Requires recent ingestion of NMDA antagonist (ketamine/PCP), neuroleptic exposure (NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, CK >1000), or serotonergic drug; toxicology and medication review usually clarifying.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with and without gadolinium to evaluate for limbic/cortical involvement and exclude mass effect, HSV encephalitis, or vascular pathology before lumbar puncture.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Often normal early; may show bilateral medial-temporal/frontobasal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion or hemorrhage; rules out HSV pattern and mass lesions.

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture with CSF analysis for cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, HSV-1/2 PCR, and a paired CSF/serum autoimmune encephalitis panel including anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, and anti-NMDAR IgG positive in CSF (gold standard; 100% sensitive, more specific than serum).

optimal_actions.action: Obtain continuous EEG monitoring to evaluate for extreme delta brush, non-convulsive status epilepticus, and overall encephalopathic background.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Abnormal in >90% of cases; extreme delta brush pattern in 30–50% (specific for anti-NMDAR encephalitis); generalized slowing; may capture electrographic seizures.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, TSH, HIV, RPR, autoimmune_encephalitis_panel, paraneoplastic_panel
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Often non-specific (mild leukocytosis, hyponatremia from SIADH); rules out infectious encephalitis, thyroid disease (Hashimoto), and other autoantibody-mediated encephalitides.

optimal_actions.action: Order contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or transvaginal ultrasound) to screen for ovarian teratoma — the trigger tumor in up to 50% of young women with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Right or left adnexal mass with mixed fat/calcification components consistent with mature cystic teratoma; if present, gynecologic-oncology resection is part of definitive therapy.

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for the Graus 2016 autoimmune-encephalitis diagnostic criteria, first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids + IVIG or plasma exchange), and second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms diagnostic criteria, treatment sequence, and emerging evidence (e.g., post-HSV NMDAR-E, checkpoint-inhibitor-associated AE) relevant to this case.

useless_tools.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must precede lumbar puncture in patients with focal neurologic signs, altered consciousness, or seizures to exclude mass effect and minimize herniation risk.

Comprehensive labs (paraneoplastic + autoimmune encephalitis panel, baseline metabolic and infectious screen) inform safe initiation of empiric immunotherapy; confirm interactions and pre-rituximab serologies before escalating.

critical_actions: Send paired CSF and serum for anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG; CSF is the gold-standard sample and must not be omitted in favor of serum-only testing.
Start empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative; HSV encephalitis is the can't-miss differential.

Initiate first-line immunotherapy promptly once clinical probability is high — IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days combined with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or therapeutic plasma exchange; do not wait for antibody results.
Screen for ovarian teratoma with pelvic imaging (transvaginal ultrasound and/or contrast-enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis); proceed to gynecologic-oncology resection if a teratoma is identified.
Control seizures aggressively with levetiracetam or valproate; obtain continuous EEG monitoring to detect non-convulsive status epilepticus.

Admit to ICU for monitoring and management of autonomic instability and central hypoventilation; escalate early to second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) if no response by day 10–14 of first-line treatment.
contraindicated_actions: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists; they worsen the movement disorder and can mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high — antibody turnaround can take 1–2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.

Do not anchor on a primary psychiatric diagnosis without first excluding autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms plus any of seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, or CSF pleocytosis.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures — exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
key_reasoning_points: The recognizable phenotype is a subacute (<3 months) progression in a young adult — viral prodrome → psychiatric/behavioral changes → seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability or decreased consciousness — fulfilling Graus 2016 criteria for probable/definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

CSF anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG is the gold-standard test (100% sensitive); serum alone is less reliable, and a negative serum result does not exclude the diagnosis. Paired CSF/serum sampling with confirmation on tissue-based assay is the standard.

Extreme delta brush on EEG is highly specific (30–50% sensitivity) for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; combined with the clinical syndrome it strongly supports the diagnosis even before antibody results return.

Treatment is time-sensitive: clinical probability should drive empiric immunotherapy (high-dose IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or plasma exchange) rather than waiting for antibody confirmation; earlier treatment correlates with better functional outcome (Titulaer 2013).

Tumor screen is part of the workup, not optional: ~50% of young women have an ovarian teratoma, and tumor removal is itself a core therapeutic step. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory in women of reproductive age.

Severe phenotypes with dysautonomia, central hypoventilation, or refractory status epilepticus require ICU-level care and earlier escalation to second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide); cardiac arrhythmias from dysautonomia justify continuous cardiac monitoring.

red_herrings.data_point: Viral prodrome (URI, fever, cough) preceding the neuropsychiatric syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Viral prodromes precede ~70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases; negative HSV PCR and the multi-stage progression should redirect the workup to anti-NMDAR antibody testing.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatremia is a recognized SIADH-mediated complication of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it should be corrected slowly and does not reframe the diagnosis.
